name: VITA shade guide
lead: The VITA classical shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs, labelled A1 to D4, that dentists hold beside a patient's teeth to describe and match tooth colour. It is arranged by value (lightness) and chroma (colour intensity), with letter groups A (red-brown), B (red-yellow), C (grey) and D (red-grey) [1]. For anyone whitening their teeth to look better, it serves as a common yardstick for saying how light teeth are before and after treatment, so a change can be described as a number of shades gained [1][4].

In looksmaxxing and cosmetic dentistry, shade numbers are shorthand for how white teeth are, and results are quoted in shade steps. Wikipedia reports in-office bleaching commonly gives about 2 to 7 shades and at-home strips or trays about 1 or 2 [1].

Dental research has examined the guide itself, including its colour coverage, the accuracy of visual matching compared with instruments, and how it compares with instruments and newer guides [2][3][8][9][10]. Many whitening trials use it as the outcome scale [4][7][12][13].

chain: Dentist or user compares teeth to numbered tabs

Whitening progress and results can be tracked and compared
angle.text: The guide does not whiten anything itself. It gives people a way to define their starting shade, set a target shade and check how much a whitening treatment has changed the look of their smile [1][4].

paras: The classical guide groups tabs by hue letter and a number for chroma. Practitioners in whitening and prosthodontics choose the tab that looks closest to a tooth under standard lighting and record its code [1]. Dental technicians receive the selected shade when they make crowns, veneers or bridges, and a Japanese review of prosthodontic teamwork notes that shade selection with the guide is often subjective and can lead to miscommunication between dentist and laboratory [11].

Digital tools, including photography, intraoral scanners and spectrophotometers, supplement or replace visual choice. A 2024 study compared shade matching by an intraoral scanner, a spectrophotometer and visual assessment [8], and another measured the in-vivo repeatability of three intra-oral spectrophotometers [9].

Researchers frequently use the guide to measure bleaching results, for example by enrolling volunteers with teeth at shade A3 or darker and counting shade steps gained [4]. Newer trials commonly report both the classical guide and the VITA Bleachedguide, in shade guide units, alongside an instrument reading [12][13].

Wikipedia lists the expected shade gains of different products: in-office 2 to 7 shades, strips and trays 1 to 2, toothpastes 1 to 2 with continued use. It also reports that nearly half of an in-office change can rebound within a week and that re-treatment may be needed every six months to a year [1].

A 1991 study examined the colour coverage of two shade guides, and a 1998 study compared a sphere spectrophotometer with human evaluation of tooth shade [2][3]. A 2025 paper titled "How many tooth colors are there?" examines the range of natural tooth colour against fixed guides [10]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small studies comparing visual, photographic and spectrophotometric matching, with 9 to 20 participants in the smaller ones and 210 patients in a 2026 study of how the order of shade presentation affects patient choice [5][6][15].
A 2014 randomised comparison examined selecting VITA classical shades using the VITA 3D-Master guide [16].

Studies have evaluated the guide as a measurement tool. A 1991 study examined coverage errors of two shade guides, and a 1998 study compared a sphere spectrophotometer with human evaluation of tooth shade [2][3]. ClinicalTrials.gov lists small trials comparing visual, photographic and spectrophotometric shade matching [5][6]. Clinical bleaching trials use the guide as an outcome scale [4][7].

Examples include a 40-person trial of in-office light-activated systems in volunteers with shade A3 or darker [4], a 2005 comparison of over-the-counter, in-office and at-home bleaching to reach six grades of whitening [7], and an 80-person randomised trial comparing combined in-office plus at-home bleaching with at-home bleaching alone, which found slightly higher colour change in the first week for the combined group, no significant difference at the end, and more sensitivity with the combined approach [12]. A 40-person split-mouth trial of 40% hydrogen peroxide found no significant colour difference between gel mixed at the session and gel mixed a week earlier [13]. A 50-person trial examined violet LED with 35% carbamide peroxide [17].

Shade numbers circulate in whitening advertisements, dentists' before-and-after galleries and online discussions of cosmetic dentistry. Regulation of the whitening products themselves differs by region: Wikipedia reports EU rules limiting retail hydrogen peroxide to 0.1% and the US FDA endorsing gels under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide [1].

card.summary: The A1-D4 tooth-colour scale dentists use to describe and track whitening results.
card.note: A measuring scale, not a treatment; visual matching accuracy varies.

quick.overview:
The VITA shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs used to name how light or dark teeth are, from A1 to D4.

It is a measurement reference, so it is used in studies and in forum talk to record whitening progress.
quick.mechanism: A clinician holds tabs next to the tooth and picks the closest match by value and chroma; instruments can also measure colour.
quick.risks: It carries no risk itself. Studies report coverage gaps in shade guides and differences between visual and instrument readings.
